name: Markovian Parallax Denigrate
title: The Internet's Oldest Gibberish Mystery
claims: Markovian Parallax Denigrate is an internet mystery involving hundreds of messages posted to Usenet in 1996 | [1]
The texts have the appearance of gibberish | [1]
The posts are often mentioned in conjunction with Sad Satan, Cicada 3301, and the Publius Enigma | [1]
Kevin Morris of The Daily Dot referred to the messages as "the Internet's oldest and weirdest mystery" in 2012 | [1]
Popmech.ru described it as "one of the first great mysteries of the Internet" | [1]
Atlas Obscura reported that all the posts had the subject line "Markovian parallax denigrate" | [1]
Ciphermysteries.com stated that the three words appeared more frequently than other words in the message bodies | [1]
The messages were posted August 5, 1996 to the alt.religion.christian.boston-church newsgroup | [1]
Susan Lindauer was mistakenly identified early on as a possible source of the posts | [1]
Kevin Morris contacted Lindauer in 2012, and she denied being the author or having any connection | [1]
An email account belonging to a University of Wisconsin at Stevens Point student named Susan Lindauer was spoofed to cover the poster's identity | [1]
Other proposed explanations include an early experimental chatbot/text generator, an internet troll/prankster posting forum spam, or a programmer experimenting with Markov chains | [1]
A 2020 article in The A.V. Club proposed the event only became a mystery due to later media coverage, not being widely reported prior to 2012 | [1]
YouTuber Barely Sociable opined that the messages were most likely simple spam with no hidden meaning | [1]
Usenet operated like a bulletin board or forum, allowing users to communicate via chronologically ordered messages | [2]
The first major spamming incident in internet history occurred in 1994 when two lawyers blasted thousands of Usenet users with immigration ads | [2]
The posts consisted of blocks of seemingly nonsensical strings of words reading like terrible slam poetry | [2]
The surviving example featured in Google's archives starts with "jitterbugging McKinley Abe" and ends with "yearbook hark" | [2]
Usenet denizens hypothesized the words were a secret code likened to Cold War numbers stations | [2]
No one has been able to detect any hidden meaning in the messages | [2]
The "Markovian" part of the name relates to a calculating process called a "Markov chain" used in programming chatbots | [2]

sources.title: The Gibberish That Sparked One of the Internet's Oldest Unsolved Mysteries - Atlas Obscura
